accuracy.evidence: Checked against the Geological Society KS3 rock cycle pages: weathering is breakdown at the surface with no movement, erosion removes and transports the bits (Erosion and Transport page), compaction squashes buried sediment under the weight of layers and cementation grows minerals between grains (Compaction and Cementation page), and metamorphic rocks were igneous or sedimentary rocks changed by heat and/or pressure without melting (Metamorphic Rocks page; marble is metamorphosed limestone). Quartz is the mineral that survives weathering into sediment and quartzite is metamorphosed sandstone, so the grain story holds. Slow cooling underground gives big crystals (granite) and fast cooling of lava gives tiny ones (basalt). Numbers checked at every corner: p2 a*100 (100..500), p4 a*1000 (3000..9000), m3 a*b (20..300), m8 a*b (10..160); rates are stated in the prompt as givens, not claimed as world values.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented slips: a fixed start or fixed order (Short cuts predict 'No: rock goes round the loop in order', challenge 'order' and 'start', m2, p5); heat and pressure confused with melting (short cut 2 rejects Magma with 'It did not melt, so it is not magma', challenge 'melt', p3); weathering confused with erosion (dragging a whole rock into the river is refused: 'too big for the river to carry. Weather it first', challenge 'erode', m1); magma called igneous rock before it cools (short cut 3 'It has not cooled yet', challenge 'cool'); new rock in a few years (Fast or slow predict 'About a few years', challenge 'fast', m6); crystal size and cooling rate (challenge 'crys', m4, m7).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagrockcyc is about the cycle itself: rocks weathered in place and carried by a river into sea-floor layers, a quartz grain moved round the five-box loop by choosing each process, three short-cut arrows drawn between boxes, five changes placed in a cross-section (mountain top, volcano, sea floor, deep underground), and six changes sorted by timescale. The Types of rock lab (flagrocktype) classifies rocks and presses one set of layers; it has no loop, no short cuts, no process choice and no timescale. The lab_distinct gate measures it under 30% against every flagship lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each idea is found by doing: a whole rock cannot go in the river until it has been weathered, so the weathering/erosion split is felt before it is named; each rock that reaches the sea adds a coloured layer; at each grain stop a wrong process is refused with what that process needs ('Melting needs rock to get hot enough deep underground'); the grain visibly returns to igneous rock; wrong short-cut boxes are explained from the story; placed changes stay labelled in their zone. Done messages state the rule only after the task.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab then disproves: 'No: it is too hard to wear away' (marble is weathered into bits and carried off like the others), 'No: rock goes round the loop in order' (the first short cut sends marble straight to sediment), and 'About a few years' (sand to sandstone sorts into the thousands-to-millions-of-years box). The correct option is second in each, so a learner cannot pass by always picking the first.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven challenge questions; every wrong option is tagged and the message names the slip: order ('Rock does not have to go round in order...'), stuck ('Every kind of rock can change'), melt ('Heat and squeezing without melting make metamorphic rock'), cool ('Igneous rock forms only when melted rock cools'), start ('a loop, so it has no start'), fast ('thousands to millions of years'), erode ('Weathering breaks rock where it stands. Erosion is when...carry the bits away'), sed and crys. In-lab feedback is specific too, quoting what each wrong box or zone means.

readability.evidence: Kid text uses short sentences and names each process once with a plain gloss ('This is called weathering'); the adult text names the age, key words, sources and mistakes; validate_lessons readability passes for learner kid (limit 6.5) and adult (limit 9.5). Canvas sentences are one short story line per stop, and every action is announced in the live region.

no_filler.evidence: Every paragraph teaches a process or a mistake; no filler phrases (the content gate passes); explanation overlap with every other lesson is under the 12% limit, including Types of rock. Practice items each test a different link of the cycle and the numeric items show how slow deposition and erosion are.

mobile.evidence: Checked on 390 px screenshots in light and dark themes: banner text wraps inside the canvas, the five boxes and arrow labels do not overlap after moving labels to the outside of the loop and shortening short-cut labels, process tiles wrap to two rows, the fast and slow boxes and cards fit, and the zone labels in the cross-section stay inside their zones. Real touch-style drags were tested: whole rock to river (refused), tap to weather, bits to river, a card into Fast.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a button: weather, put whole rock in river, pick up bits, each process, each box, each place and each card; the canvas aria-label is updated with every message; walk.cjs reports axe WCAG 2.1 AA clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13, with every task completed by Show me and no console errors.
